notes.title: The four Books of Kings
notes.text: These are the books now commonly called 1 and 2 Samuel and 1 and 2 Kings. The author says he has already retold the history they cover, from the rise of the monarchy to Jerusalem’s fall to Babylon. The surviving work starts later, with the Maccabees.

notes.title: The prophecy about the Maccabees
notes.text: Klebs takes the brief “prophetic account” to mean Daniel 11. That chapter describes a king who violates the sanctuary and a group that resists him. On this reading, the king is Antiochus IV and the resistance is the beginning of the Maccabean revolt.

notes.title: The line of Judah
notes.text: The author reads Jacob’s blessing of Judah as a promise about who would rule the Jewish people. Gualtherus takes Herod’s accession as the decisive break because Herod came from an Idumaean family. He treats the intervening rule of the Maccabees, a priestly family, as a complication in tracing that line.

notes.title: Rulers after the exile
notes.text: In Gualtherus’s account, the descendants of David are styled governors after the Babylonian exile. He names Zerubbabel as the leader who brought the people back to Jerusalem under Persian rule. This is one of the changes of government the author has to reckon with in tracing the line of Judah.

Josephus (BI I 31) begins with strife among powerful Jews and the conflict between Antiochus and Ptolemy.

notes.text: The Hasideans are the fighting men who join Mattathias. In 1 Maccabees they are volunteers committed to defending Jewish law. The same chapter explains the decision to fight on the Sabbath in self-defense, after a group who refused to fight was killed.

notes.text: The trap is set by Tryphon, a Seleucid commander. He offers Jonathan friendship, persuades him to send most of his men away, and takes him prisoner at Ptolemais. The Latin compresses that sequence into the offer of friendship and Jonathan’s confinement and death.

notes.title: Antiochus and the siege
notes.text: The Antiochus who besieges John Hyrcanus is the brother of Demetrius II Nicator, known as Antiochus VII Sidetes. The treasure story explains how Hyrcanus is said to have paid him off. Of the 3,000 talents supposedly taken from David’s tomb, the Latin puts the payment at 300.

notes.title: Why Mundus brings up Alcmene and Leda
notes.text: In Greek myth, Zeus had children with mortal women. Alcmene was the mother of Heracles, and Leda was associated with the birth of Helen. The man impersonating Anubis uses these familiar stories to persuade Paulina that a god could father a child with her. The mythological examples are additions in the Latin retelling.

Agrippa brings in their story as he describes the African lands now under Rome.

notes.title: Where Berenice watches
notes.text: The Xystus is a public space near the Temple. Agrippa speaks there before the crowd. His sister Berenice watches from a conspicuous position above the crowd. In Josephus’s account both siblings weep, and their tears help to quiet the assembly.

notes.title: Why the Jews of Scythopolis leave the city
notes.text: The narrative turns from Damascus to an earlier massacre at Scythopolis. The Jews who live there side with their neighbors against Jewish raiders, but are asked to leave the city to prove their loyalty. Two quiet nights lead them to relax their guard. The townspeople attack on the third night.

IX, 34. “Aenea, sanat (ἰᾶται) te Dominus Jesus Christus: surge et sterne tibi.” From this passage in Acts it appears that Ambrose wrote the indicative sanat here too, in place of the precative sanet. notes.text: This is the reading of the usual printed editions. Gualtherus, however, reports in his notes that he found Non hominem somewhere. In my judgment this is by far the best reading and the only correct one. Simon persuaded credulous people that he was Dei potentiam, or divine power, as is clear from Act. VIII, 10. So when the crowd saw him flying, it quite naturally cried out Dei esse potentiam, Non hominem. The entire sentence should therefore be corrected and punctuated as follows, unless I am mistaken. “Mirari populus et venerari: plerique dicentes (eum) Dei esse potentiam, non hominem, qui cum corpore volitaret.” [Mazochius] l. c. pag. 863.

notes.text: There can be no doubt that celebrare orationem here means “to offer the sacrifice of the Mass” in Ambrose's usage. The Acts of St. Pionius the martyr in Ruinart, sect. 5, describe his arrest with his companions after the events recounted in “Facta ergo ORATIONE solemni cum die sabbato SANCTUM PANEM et aquam degustavissent”. In can. 13 of the Council of Laodicea, Dionysius's translation reads “Presbyteri ruris, episcopo praesente, vel presbyteri urbis ipsius, offerre non possunt, neque panem sanctificatum dare calicemque porrigere. Si vero absentes hi fuerint, et (εἰς εὐχὴν) ad dandam orationem vocentur, soli dare debebunt”. For the words about giving the consecrated bread, the Greek has οὔτε μὴν ἄρτον διδόναι ἐν Ε ΥΧΗ , literally nec panem dare in ORATIONE. In his commentary on the canon Zonaras explains ἐν εὐχῆ as ἐν ἱερουγίας καιρῶ. tempore sacrificii. Thus in the Greek liturgical books Μυστικὴ εὐχὴ, Mystica oratio, corresponds to what we call Missam. Balsamon, commenting on Gregory of Nyssa's letter to Letoius, takes μυστικῆς ἐπιτελουμέμης εὐχῆς, to refer to the consecration of the bread and chalice, before which the priest says a private prayer for their sanctification. [Mazochius] l. c. pag. 993.

notes.title: The date of the Temple fire
notes.text: Lous is a Macedonian month name, corresponding roughly to August. The tenth day is already ill-omened because, in Josephus’s account, the earlier Temple had been burned by the Babylonians on the same date.

notes.text: Suidas identifies Loum with the Macedonian month corresponding to August. [de La Barre] See Dodwell, de Cyclis veter. Graec. et Roman. dissert. 9, pag. 397, for a comparison of the Macedonian and Hebrew months on the evidence of Josephus. The Macedonian Lous, however, is July. Even so, Suidas need not have been mistaken. The lexicographer presumably meant the Syro-Macedonians. Scholars recognize that the Macedonian year begins a month before theirs, so that Λῶος, which is July for the Macedonians, is August for the Syro-Macedonians. Fabricius discusses this well in his Menologio, pagg. 43, 45. [Gallandi]

notes.title: The lamb and the open gate
notes.text: The reported birth is a lamb from a cow being led to sacrifice. The same sequence tells of the heavy bronze gate on the east side of the inner court opening by itself, although it usually takes twenty men to shut it. Some see the opening as a good sign. Others take it to mean that the Temple is exposed.

notes.title: The survivors at Masada
notes.text: Josephus says that one of the women who survived was a relative of Eleazar and the other was an older woman. They hid with five children in the underground channels that carried drinking water. In the Latin it is one surviving woman who tells the Romans what happened.
notes.html: Josephus says that one of the women who survived was a relative of Eleazar and the other was an older woman. They hid with five children in the underground channels that carried drinking water. In the Latin it is one surviving woman who tells the Romans what happened.
